st: Cut the potatoes into chips about 0.75 inch thick. Soak in cold water for 20 minutes, then drain and dry very well.
Heat [[8 cups]] oil in a heavy pot to 300°F (150°C). Fry the chips in batches for 6 minutes until pale and soft. Drain.
Pat the fish dry and season with [[1 tsp]] salt. Dust with [[0.25 cup]] flour.
Whisk [[1.5 cups]] flour, [[1 tsp]] baking powder, and [[0.5 tsp]] salt, then whisk in [[1 cup]] cold beer until smooth.
Raise the oil to 375°F (190°C). Dip a fish piece in the batter, let the extra drip off, and lower it into the oil away from you.
Fry for 6 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and the fish flakes at 145°F (63°C). Drain on a rack.
Fry the chips again for 3 minutes until crisp and golden, then drain and salt with [[1 tsp]] salt.
Serve at once with lemon wedges and vinegar.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] oil in a large skillet over medium-low heat. Add the sausages and cook for 15 minutes, turning, until browned and at least 160°F (71°C).
Meanwhile, pour the beans into a small pot and warm them over low heat, stirring now and then.
Move the sausages to a warm plate. Fry the bacon in the same pan for 4 minutes until crisp. Set aside.
Place the tomatoes cut side down in the pan and fry for 3 minutes. Add the mushrooms and cook for 4 minutes with a pinch of salt.
Push everything to a warm plate. Melt [[1 tbsp]] butter in the pan and fry the eggs for 3 minutes, until the whites are set.
Toast the bread and spread with the remaining [[1 tbsp]] butter.
Season with [[0.5 tsp]] salt and [[0.25 tsp]] pepper. Plate everything with the beans and toast while hot.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). Rub the beef with [[1 tbsp]] oil, [[1 tsp]] salt, and [[1 tsp]] pepper and let it sit for 30 minutes.
Roast the beef for 15 minutes, then lower the oven to 350°F (175°C) and roast for 60 minutes more, until 135°F (57°C) in the center for medium-rare.
Parboil the potatoes in salted water for 8 minutes, drain, and shake them in the pot to roughen the edges.
Toss the potatoes with [[3 tbsp]] oil and roast on a tray for 50 minutes, turning once, with the carrots alongside.
Whisk [[1 cup]] flour, 3 eggs, [[1 cup]] milk, and [[0.5 tsp]] salt into a smooth batter and rest it.
Take out the beef and rest it for 20 minutes under foil. Raise the oven to 450°F (230°C).
Put [[1 tsp]] oil in each cup of a 12-cup muffin pan and heat for 5 minutes until smoking hot. Fill each cup half full with batter.
Bake the puddings for 18 minutes until tall and golden. Do not open the door early.
Slice the beef and serve with the potatoes, carrots, puddings, and warm gravy.
Boil the potatoes in salted water for 18 minutes until very tender. Drain.
Mash with [[3 tbsp]] butter, [[0.25 cup]] warm milk, and [[1 tsp]] salt until smooth.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Brown the lamb in a large oven-safe skillet for 8 minutes until cooked through at 160°F (71°C). Drain extra fat.
Add the remaining [[1 tbsp]] butter, the onion, and the carrots. Cook for 6 minutes until soft.
Stir in [[2 tbsp]] tomato paste and [[2 tbsp]] flour for 1 minute, then add [[1 cup]] broth, the Worcestershire, [[1 tsp]] salt, and the pepper.
Simmer for 10 minutes until thick, then stir in the peas.
Spread the mashed potatoes over the filling and roughen the top with a fork.
Bake for 25 minutes until the top is golden and the edges bubble. Rest for 10 minutes.

ing: or beef broth thickened as below
st: Boil the potatoes in salted water for 18 minutes until a knife slides in easily. Drain.
Meanwhile, brown the sausages in [[1 tbsp]] oil in a skillet over medium heat for 15 minutes, turning, until at least 160°F (71°C).
Move the sausages to a plate. Cook the onions in the same pan with [[1 tbsp]] butter for 12 minutes until soft and golden.
Sprinkle the onions with [[1 tbsp]] flour, stir for 1 minute, then pour in [[1.5 cups]] gravy or broth.
Simmer for 5 minutes until thick, then return the sausages to the pan.
Mash the potatoes with [[3 tbsp]] butter, [[0.5 cup]] warm milk, [[1 tsp]] salt, and [[0.5 tsp]] pepper until smooth.
Pile the mash on plates, lay the sausages on top, and spoon over the onion gravy.
Whisk [[1 cup]] flour and [[0.5 tsp]] salt in a bowl. Make a well in the middle.
Crack in the eggs and add a splash of the milk. Whisk until smooth.
Whisk in the rest of the [[1 cup]] milk to make a thin batter.
Rest the batter at room temperature for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). Put [[0.5 tbsp]] oil in each of 12 muffin cups.
Heat the pan in the oven for 5 minutes until the oil is smoking hot.
Pour the batter into the hot cups, about half full. Close the door fast.
Bake for 20 minutes without opening the oven until puffed, deep golden, and crisp. Serve right away.
Mix [[3 cups]] flour and [[1 tsp]] salt. Rub in [[0.75 cup]] cold butter until crumbly, then stir in the ice water to form a dough.
Wrap the dough and chill for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Mix the beef, potatoes, swede, onion, [[1 tsp]] salt, and [[1 tsp]] pepper in a bowl.
Divide the dough in 4 and roll each into an 8-inch circle.
Pile the filling onto one half of each circle, leaving a border.
Brush the border with water, fold the dough over, and crimp the edge into a rope pattern.
Place on a lined tray, brush with beaten egg, and cut a small vent in the top.
Bake for 20 minutes, then lower to 350°F (175°C) and bake for 40 minutes more. The beef must reach 160°F (71°C).
Cool for 10 minutes before eating.
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment.
Mix [[2.5 cups]] flour, [[1 tbsp]] baking powder, [[3 tbsp]] sugar, and [[0.25 tsp]] salt.
Rub in [[0.5 cup]] cold butter with your fingertips until the mix looks like breadcrumbs.
Pour in [[0.75 cup]] milk and stir with a knife until a soft dough forms. Do not overwork it.
Pat the dough out on a floured counter to 1 inch thick.
Cut rounds with a 2.5-inch cutter, pressing straight down and not twisting. Place on the tray.
Brush the tops with [[1 tbsp]] milk and bake for 14 minutes until risen and golden.
Cool for 10 minutes, split, and top with [[0.5 cup]] jam and [[0.75 cup]] clotted cream.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and grease a 9-inch square pan.
Pour [[1 cup]] boiling water over the dates and [[1 tsp]] baking soda. Let sit for 15 minutes.
Cream [[0.5 cup]] of the soft butter with [[0.75 cup]] brown sugar until fluffy. Beat in the eggs and vanilla.
Fold in [[1.5 cups]] flour, [[1.5 tsp]] baking powder, and the salt. Stir in the dates with their liquid.
Pour into the pan and bake for 35 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.
Meanwhile, melt the other [[0.5 cup]] butter with [[1 cup]] dark brown sugar and [[1 cup]] cream in a pan. Simmer for 5 minutes, stirring, until smooth.
Poke holes in the warm cake and pour over a third of the sauce. Cut into squares.
Serve warm with the remaining sauce.
Season the beef with [[1 tsp]] salt and [[1 tsp]] pepper. Sear in [[1 tbsp]] hot oil in a pan for 1 minute on each side. Brush with mustard and cool.
Cook the mushrooms in [[1 tbsp]] oil with the thyme and [[0.5 tsp]] salt for 12 minutes until dry and browned. Cool.
Lay plastic wrap on the counter and overlap the prosciutto. Spread with the mushrooms.
Place the beef on top and roll up tightly in the plastic. Chill for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Roll out the pastry and unwrap the beef onto it.
Fold the pastry around the beef, trimming extra, and seal the seam. Brush with beaten egg and score lightly.
Place seam down on a tray and chill for 15 minutes.
Bake for 35 minutes until golden, to 125°F (52°C) for rare or 135°F (57°C) for medium-rare inside.
Rest for 10 minutes, then cut into thick slices.
Pour the roast drippings into a saucepan, leaving the browned bits, and heat over medium heat.
Add the chopped onion and cook for 4 minutes until soft.
Sprinkle in [[3 tbsp]] flour and stir for 2 minutes until it turns golden brown.
Slowly pour in [[2 cups]] hot stock, whisking all the time, to avoid lumps.
Add the Worcestershire, [[0.5 tsp]] salt, and [[0.25 tsp]] pepper.
Simmer for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon.
Taste, add salt if needed, and strain if you want it smooth. Serve hot.
Wash the mint and pat the leaves dry. Remove the stems.
Dissolve [[1 tbsp]] sugar in [[2 tbsp]] boiling water in a small bowl.
Chop the mint very finely on a board with a sharp knife.
Add the mint and a pinch of salt to the sugar water.
Stir in [[3 tbsp]] vinegar.
Let the sauce stand for 10 minutes so the flavors come together.
Taste and add more sugar or vinegar to balance, then serve with roast lamb.
Boil the eggs for 10 minutes until the yolks are fully set, then cool in cold water and peel. This is the only cooking, and fully cooked eggs are safe to serve.
Take the cheddar out of the fridge 30 minutes before serving so it softens and its sharp flavor opens up.
Cut the cheddar into a thick wedge and the Red Leicester into slabs. Keep the pieces large because a ploughman's is not dainty.
Fold the ham slices over once and lay them beside the cheese. Slice the bread and spread it with [[3 tbsp]] butter.
Spoon [[3 tbsp]] Branston pickle into a small dish and set the pickled onions next to it. Cut the eggs in half.
Slice the apple just before serving so it does not brown. Add it with the celery sticks and serve on a plate or board.
nt: Don't cook except boiling the eggs: slice, fold, arrange; cheddar at room temperature 30 minutes
Best swap: Wensleydale or Double Gloucester for the cheddar; vegetarians skip the ham and double the cheese and eggs.

st: Heat the oven to 325°F. Line an 8 inch round cake pan with parchment.
Rub [[1 cup]] cold butter into [[2 cups]] flour, [[0.25 cup]] rice flour, [[0.5 cup]] sugar and a pinch of salt with your fingertips until it looks like fine crumbs.
Press the crumbs together and knead briefly, just until a smooth dough forms. Overworking makes it tough.
Press the dough evenly into the pan and smooth the top. Prick all over with a fork and score into 8 wedges.
Chill the pan for 20 minutes so the shortbread holds its shape in the oven.
Bake 40 minutes until pale golden at the edges. Sprinkle with [[1 tbsp]] sugar straight away.
Re-cut the wedges while warm. Cool completely in the pan before lifting out.
nt: Best swap: vegan butter sticks 1:1 for the butter, keeping it cold, for a dairy-free version.

ing: cold for pastry plus softened for filling, divided
st: Rub [[0.5 cup]] cold cubed butter into the flour with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs, then stir in [[3 tbsp]] ice water to make a dough. Wrap and chill for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 375°F. Roll the dough to 1/8 inch thick and press it into a 9 inch tart tin. Prick the base with a fork and chill 10 minutes.
Line the shell with parchment and baking beans and bake for 15 minutes. Remove the parchment and bake 5 minutes more until pale gold.
Spread the jam in an even layer over the warm base.
Beat [[0.25 cup]] softened butter with the sugar until pale. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then fold in the ground almonds and almond extract.
Spoon the frangipane over the jam and smooth the top. Scatter the sliced almonds over it.
Bake for 30 minutes until puffed, golden and a skewer comes out clean. Cool completely in the tin.
Stir the powdered sugar with [[2 tsp]] water, drizzle over the cooled tart and let it set for 10 minutes before slicing.
nt: Best swap: use almond flour in place of ground almonds 1 to 1, or any jam you like in place of raspberry.

st: Put the haddock in a wide pan with the milk, water and bay leaf. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat and poach 6 to 8 minutes until the fish flakes easily.
Lift the fish onto a plate. Strain the poaching liquid and keep it. Remove skin and bones from the fish and flake it into large chunks.
Melt the butter in a clean pot over medium-low heat. Cook the onion for 5 minutes until soft but not browned.
Add the potatoes and the strained poaching liquid. Simmer for 15 minutes until the potatoes are very tender.
Mash about a third of the potatoes against the side of the pot with a spoon to thicken the soup, leaving the rest in chunks.
Fold in the flaked haddock and warm for 2 minutes. Season with pepper, taste before adding any salt as the fish is salty, and stir in the parsley.
nt: Poached in milk, then simmered as a chowder
Best swap: any other smoked white fish such as smoked cod or pollock 1:1; for dairy-free use unsweetened oat milk.

ing: cold smoked herring, about 6 oz each
st: Boil a kettle of water. Place the kippers skin side down in a deep dish or tall jug and cover completely with the boiling water.
Leave for 5 minutes to warm the fish through and soften the smoky saltiness. Lift out with a spatula and drain on paper towels.
Melt the butter in a skillet over medium heat until foaming, then slide in the kippers skin side down.
Cook for 2 minutes per side, spooning the butter over, until the flesh flakes easily and is hot in the center.
Transfer to warm plates, pour over the browned butter and scatter with parsley and pepper.
Serve with buttered brown bread, lemon wedges and a poached egg on top if you like. Watch for fine bones as you eat.
nt: Poached in hot water, then pan-fried in butter
Best swap: smoked mackerel fillets work the same way, or grill the kippers under a hot broiler for 4 minutes with a brush of butter.

st: Heat the oven to 300°F. Line an 8 inch round deep pan with a double layer of parchment.
Beat the butter and brown sugar for 4 minutes until fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time, with a spoonful of flour to stop curdling.
Fold in the rest of the flour, baking powder and spice, then the dried fruit and peel.
Roll [[0.5 lb]] marzipan into an 8 inch disc. Put half the batter in the pan, lay the disc on top and cover with the remaining batter.
Bake for 2 hours 15 minutes until a skewer comes out clean. Cover the top with foil if it browns too fast.
Cool fully in the pan. Brush the top with warm apricot jam.
Roll [[0.5 lb]] marzipan into an 8 inch round and press onto the jam. Crimp the edges with your fingers.
Roll the remaining marzipan into 11 balls for the apostles and press them evenly around the edge.
Brown the marzipan topping under a hot grill for 1 to 2 minutes, watching closely, until lightly toasted.
nt: Best swap: almond paste mixed with powdered sugar for marzipan; raisins only if you lack mixed fruit.

st: Set a heatproof bowl over a pot of barely simmering water. The bowl must not touch the water.
Add the lemon zest, [[0.5 cup]] strained lemon juice, sugar and butter to the bowl and stir until the butter melts.
Whisk the eggs and yolk in a separate bowl, then pour them through a sieve into the bowl.
Cook, whisking constantly, for 10 minutes until the curd reaches 170°F and coats the back of a spoon. This cooks the eggs fully.
Remove from the heat and strain through a fine sieve to remove any bits of cooked egg.
Press plastic wrap onto the surface and chill for 2 hours until set. Keeps 2 weeks in the fridge.
nt: Gently cooked over a double boiler
Best swap: lime or Meyer lemon juice at the same amount, or plant butter for dairy-free.

st: Mix the raisins, currants, peel and [[0.25 cup]] brandy in a large bowl. Cover and soak for at least 1 hour, or overnight for the best flavor.
Stir in the breadcrumbs, flour, sugar, suet, grated apple, spice, zest and salt until evenly blended.
Add the beaten eggs and mix well. The batter should drop slowly from a spoon. Everyone in the house traditionally takes a turn stirring and makes a wish.
Butter a 1.5 quart pudding basin. Spoon the mix in and press it down, leaving 1 inch of space at the top for the pudding to rise.
Cover with a layer of pleated parchment then foil. Tie tightly with string, adding a string handle so you can lift it out.
Set the basin on a rack in a large pot and pour in boiling water to halfway up the bowl. Cover and simmer gently for 5 hours, topping up with boiling water as needed.
Cool, re-wrap and store somewhere cool for up to a month. On Christmas Day, steam 1.5 hours to reheat. Warm [[2 tbsp]] brandy, pour it over, and light it.
nt: Steamed in a basin for about five hours
Best swap: use cold grated butter at the same amount for the suet to make it vegetarian.

st: Rub [[6 tbsp]] butter and the lard into [[2.5 cup]] flour with [[0.5 tsp]] salt until it looks like crumbs. Add [[0.5 cup]] cold water and bring together. Rest 30 minutes in the fridge.
Heat the oven to 400°F. Mix the beef, suet, onion, [[1 tsp]] salt and the pepper in a bowl. Do not add liquid; the suet makes the gravy.
Roll the dough 0.25 inch thick and cut four ovals about 7 by 5 inches.
Pile the filling on one half of each oval, leaving a 1 inch rim. Brush the rim with beaten egg.
Fold the other half over and crimp the edge firmly with a fork. Cut a small steam hole in the top and brush with egg.
Bake on a lined tray 20 minutes, then lower the heat to 350°F and bake 25 minutes more until golden and the beef is cooked through. Serve hot.
nt: Best swap: use 2 tbsp cold butter plus 1 tbsp cold water in place of the suet, or use beef stock cubes dissolved in 2 tbsp water for moisture.
